Don’t know where this is going, posted this somewhere I hope, read and you will understand. Also, I hope some of you are tech savvy because some of it will be a bit complicated.

The long and short of it all is that I made something. Well in truth I didn’t actually make it, it kind of made itself, but I will explain that soon enough. I am a college student currently studying computing machines at a fairly good school and now that we are on break I have a lot of time on my hands. I have always been interested in AI and artificial learning systems but none of my classes really gave me real satisfaction on the topic, we covered some learning algorithms but most of the rest of the class was pre-programmed responses and probability based actions and responses. Kind of interesting but again, it is all just what the creator initially codes, nothing that new.

When you say the word Artificial Intelligence it conjures up the idea of a program or robot that has ideas, direction, perhaps consciousness. The technology and understanding is nowhere near being able to create such things artificially yet, hell we don’t even understand how they work in us, but that doesn’t mean such things are beyond us. To create an artificial life form that could mimic and even rival traditional notions of life one could employ the same tool used by nature itself.

I am not an expert on the ideas behind abiogenisis, much less creating them in an artificial environment, so I decided I could clear the first hurdle and program the first little digital microorganism, the first ‘life’ by myself. Like traditional forms of life, and to follow the ideas of evolution it had to have a kind of ‘food source’, reproduction, mortality, and mutation.

The food source was simple, I decided the thing would ‘feed’ of .jpg and .png file types. when I say feed I don’t mean in the traditional sense of nutrition because they didn’t technically need it to survive. I created in part of the main function a food requirement that grew as a function of processor ticks in whatever machine it was currently residing in. I would scan an image and acquire resource points, and it could spend said points by traveling to a new destination or opening a new file. It also received more resource points the larger the picture got (up to about 10KB because beyond that the program ran the risk of being noticed due to high memory usage when the program ‘scanned it’) Reproduction was similarly simple, there were no male or female programs -any could reproduce with any other- and would reproduce by combining the code of any two programs. The programs would take turns writing byte by byte into a .txt file saved inside one of the reproducing program’s folders and after the information was exchanged a mutator would go through and randomly change bytes of data inside the code which was to become the machine code once compiled. The tricky part here, and the main dividing line between chemical evolution and ‘artificial’ evolution is that computer code is delicate, and 999 times out of 1000 the mutation will only create a program that doesn’t run or has a critical error. Therefore the amount of reproduction that has to take place is huge to offset the high ‘infant mortality rate’ I made it so the code would create 5,000 copies for every resource point the ‘pregnant’ program had (~30-50). After that the ‘pregnant’ program would execute each batch of code a hundred at a time to keep things small, letting free all that survived. Mortality was a simpler problem. Every program would quit once either it’s resource counter went below zero, it was deleted by a virus scan, or it’s inbuilt mortality clock ran out. Usually the things would last about 200 billion cycles or about a minute on a good processor running about 3 Ghz. the first batch was run in a sandbox on my computer and lasted about thirty minutes before it filled the allocated memory (glad I thought to restrict it beforehand) and crashed. I also added a time delay here so that every program couldn’t just eat one image all the time. I made it so the first five pixels’ color values were stored in memory which would make it so an image couldn’t be until the next generation. Over the course of the next few days I tweaked the settings until I got a population with death/reproduction rates that were stable. Life was nice for the little ‘Omegas’ in that period, but eventually in every simulation the mutation would gradually favor increased resource points and fewer deaths which unfailingly reached allotted memory. I decided that since some of them ousted the death code altogether I should make some aspects unchangeable and add a kind of ultimate death. To do this I made it so the death function would read in a file outside the program itself which would have the code for the death function and could not be rewritten on reproduction. To keep them from avoiding them from reading in the program altogether I made it so the pointers for the function of move/ reproduce/ feed/ etc. were only accessible via a hash table on the death file. So no death, no life. This fixed the problems with the program making itself immortal but I still wanted to have some more fun, so I designed a predator. They were basically the same as the ‘omegas’ but they got resource points from a dead omega (based on how many the omega had) and when they encountered one they would rewrite all the memory the program was using basically scrambling and killing it without needing an alternate function that could be mutated out of. It took me two days of trial and error to figure out starting levels where both populations could be stable but once I did it felt great.

This is where things got sketchy.

I decided to let the program run overnight and see if the populations were still stable in more long term conditions. I turned on the simulation and went to bed imagining that one would either win out or die off by the time I woke up. Neither happened. I woke up to my computer repeating the windows error sound and a troubling series of error messages from a data defender, virus scanner, and the OS itself, the last message saying “warning, low on memory.”

I exited out of the errors but when I closed down the simulation the errors came right back up. A look at current processes revealed that there were at least four thousand copies of omegas and alphas all running not on the sandbox, but on OS itself. Sometime in the night, one little omega managed to accidentally break free of the sandbox and it flourished in the predator free environment. The resulting generations were able to then bypass all security features and eventually nearly used up all the memory in their rampant reproduction. I tried closing them down one by one but there were so many I knew that would never work long term. I decided to do the one thing I could think of and started a batch of 100 predators in the OS in hopes to bring both of their numbers down to manageable levels. What I witnessed next was equal parts terrifying and beautiful. With each generation lasting a little over a minute it was like watching everything in fast forward. Hunting and evasion pattern began to evolve over the course of a few hours I spent glued to the screen. some omegas clustered in folders and became so isolated from others that they evolved past viable reproduction with each other, some predators or ‘alphas’ did the same by selectively hunting only certain omegas. I was watching species form and change right before my very eyes. It felt indescribable.

I wanted to shut it down but it was far out of my control at this point, and even if it was I don’t know if I could have brought myself to do it. It was so incredible in a way. About three hours in I noticed a distinct pattern beginning to emerge within a pattern of omegas that seemed to be getting food without eating. They would disappear off the system for a few seconds and then reappear with far more resource points. It took me a minute before I realized what It was doing. I stupidly forgot to unplug the computer and the little buggers had gotten on the network. I hurriedly unplugged the machine but I figured enough had already got out. all I could see was what they had created on my own computer, a network of species with code so altered and complex and diluted I could hardly tell what any of it even did. The creatures were detected a few times but they quickly evolved the ability to remain hidden on most every system. they changed and mutated over months and months inside a universe of their own creation. The txt file that I had created to enforce death initially was now a huge series of folders outlining a universe of which every creature followed. They had senses, vision, hearing, touch, all within a million circuits and transistors. I tried to distance myself from the project so hopefully the government can’t find me when this all goes down but I don’t know anymore. Last week I found a new creature that seems to be different than all the others. Using the separate ‘death’ file as a kind of roadmap I found that the area is described as ‘hot’ and ‘grassy’ whatever that means. I watched the creature move and change as it rapidly shifted the landscape of organisms and began to change the world around it. It used tools, it created machines, it thought. Last night I found a cluster of them on my own computer and as I tried to open up and examine their files I heard the sound of a million voices speaking in a strange language begin to drift out of my speakers.

OUR FATHER, WHO ART IN HEAVEN

HALLOWED BE THY NAME

DISCLAIMER - The traffic stop was made in 2000 (according to the author, Moskos). For you mobile goats, here's the article in full (sorry paywall, but ad clickies will have to do for your salary for now).

Early one December morning in East Baltimore in 2000, I saw a car drive by with its headlights off. For minor traffic violations, for honest mistakes — if the driver was sober, polite and carrying a valid license and registration — I would usually just issue a warning.

I stopped the car. But before I could get on the police radio to call in the stop, the driver — a very agitated middle-aged African American woman, and seemingly middle-class — exited the car while shouting into her cellphone. She ended one call and made another. The “routine” went out of this 1 a.m. stop.

I told her to get back in her car several times, which she finally did reluctantly . I approached and asked for her license. She was on her phone saying she wanted a sergeant and another officer and added: “If I’m going to get shot, I want it to be recorded because I know this is recorded and I know my rights . . . if I get shot, I want it documented.”

She wouldn’t stop talking, yelling really, at me and into her phone : “He just pulled me over for being black. I can’t believe this would happen to me. There are all those drug dealers, and you’ve got to harass me!” I could see the parking lights on her dashboard were illuminated, which maybe made her think her headlights were on. I pointed this out to her. She said, ignoring my point, that she was on her way to donate suitcases for charity. After a few more requests, she gave me her license.

As I returned to my car, a call came over the radio for a woman being assaulted by a police officer at my location. I told the dispatcher there was no assault in progress, and the call was related to my traffic stop. Before I had even approached her, much less spoken to her, she had called 911, aggrieved, certain of the injustice she was experiencing at the hands of a white officer.

I thought of this stop while watching the video of Sandra Bland, the young woman who died in jail after she was stopped in Texas for an illegal lane change, a minor violation. Like that scenario, my traffic stop could have gone in any number of directions.

Legally, morally and tactically, I had many options and tools at my disposal. I could have raised my voice. I could have issued more orders. I could have threatened the woman with force and arrested her for non-compliance. I could have done all that legally, but I didn’t want to. What is legally permitted is not always morally acceptable. I didn’t want to start a physical altercation because there’s always a chance you’ll lose.

I was on guard but not afraid. I was focused on a goal: to finish this stop without anybody getting injured. Honestly, I had little sympathy for this woman’s mistaken sense of moral justice. But I had empathy for her as a human being. And other things being equal, I’d prefer not to wrestle and handcuff a middle-aged woman for a minor traffic violation, no matter the legal justification. I could win tactically but not morally.

My sergeant, a bit baffled, and another officer, more simply amused, arrived on the scene within minutes. After a brief summary from me, my sergeant told me to remain near my car while he approached and talked to the woman. I filled in a ticket to give her. Ironically, given her insistence that I stopped her only because she was black (in a neighborhood that is 98 percent African American), a verbal warning could be used as proof that the stop was unjustified. I needed a paper trail to cover my actions.

The driver remained upset, glaring while she signed for the ticket: “I had my lights on. How can you look me in the eye and tell me I didn’t have my lights on? God will judge you. You’ll have to answer to God in the end!”

In the end, we had only a traffic court judge to answer to. He listened to our versions of the stop before concluding, “Sounds like a routine traffic stop. . . . I’ll take the officer’s word over yours. Guilty.”

Was that the ideal ending? I don’t know. Little about policing is ideal. But that’s why we have police officers, to handle non-ideal situations. These often involve people who are lost, mentally ill, criminals or victims. And, like Sandra Bland, nobody should die because police officers are more interested in absolute dominance than professional, moral and tactical discretion. Peaceful resolution isn’t just the right thing to do — it’s the very purpose of policing.
